transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, mostly it’s the sleeping, doctor. I just don’t sleep right anymore. I’ll go to bed and I’m tired, I know I’m tired, but then I just lay there for what feels like a long time, staring off and waiting for sleep to come. And then when I finally do drift off, it doesn’t feel like good sleep.

I wake up from bad dreams sometimes, or even just little noises — things that maybe shouldn’t bother a person that much — and once I’m awake, that’s it for a while. I can’t seem to settle myself back down. I’ll turn this way and that, try to get comfortable, try to tell myself it’s nothing, but my body just won’t listen. So that’s why I came in, really. It’s been wearing on me.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things during the day?

Yes… I do. Maybe not worry in the way I used to think of worrying, like about bills or appointments or whether I left something on the stove. It’s more like… I don’t trust ordinary things the same anymore.

I know it probably sounds foolish when I say it out loud, but during the day I’ll catch myself thinking that everyday things aren’t really safe. Simple things that other people don’t think twice about, I start feeling like if I let my guard down or trust them, they’ll turn on me somehow. And I can tell myself, “That doesn’t make sense,” but it still sits there in my mind.

It’s tiring, because it makes the day feel… uneasy, I guess. Like I’m always waiting for something ordinary to become a problem.
Do you experience any physical sensations, like pain or tension, when you're feeling uneasy or on guard?

Yes… I think so. It’s hard for me to separate what’s in my body from what’s in my head, if that makes sense. When I’m uneasy, I don’t just think about things — I start checking them.

Like if I go somewhere now, even a regular place, I catch myself looking around before I can relax. I look up at things, wondering what might fall. I look for the exits, where I’d go if I had to get out. And I pay attention to the floor, or the steps, whether they look steady, whether there’s something loose or uneven there.

I don’t always mean to do it. It’s just like my body won’t let me sit easy until I’ve looked everything over. Then maybe I can settle a little, but even then I’m still sort of watching.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places or activities because of these feelings of unease?

Yes… yes, I think I do. I don’t always call it avoiding, because I’ll make it sound more reasonable in my own head, you know? I’ll tell myself I’m just tired, or the weather’s not right, or I’ve got something else to do around the house.

But I keep finding reasons not to go down to the senior center. I used to go more, just to be around people a bit, sit and talk, maybe have coffee. Now I’ll get ready like I might go, and then I start thinking about it too much, and pretty soon I’ve talked myself out of it.

And the garage is another one. I don’t like being out there the way I used to. Especially around the tools… and over near where I used to keep that ladder. I’ll say, “Well, that can wait,” or “I don’t need to fool with that today,” but truthfully, I just don’t want to be near it. I can feel myself getting uneasy before I even get started, so I just shut the door and leave it alone.
Do you ever feel like you have to repeat certain actions or rituals to help you feel safer or less uneasy?

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean, maybe.

I mean, I’ll check things, like I said before, and sometimes I might look at something more than once because I don’t quite believe myself the first time. But I don’t have, like, a set thing I do over and over, if that’s what you’re asking. No counting or touching things a certain number of times, nothing like that.

It’s more that I hesitate. I’ll stand there longer than I probably need to, looking something over, trying to feel sure. But I don’t know if I’d call that a ritual. It doesn’t feel organized like that. It’s just me trying to settle myself down, I guess, and sometimes it works a little, sometimes it doesn’t.
Are there any specific objects or situations that consistently make you feel uneasy?

Yes… there are. I guess the two that come to mind right away are the senior center and my garage.

The senior center sounds harmless when I say it out loud, and I know that. It’s just a place where people sit around, talk, have coffee, maybe play cards. But I keep finding reasons not to go. I’ll think, “Well, maybe tomorrow,” or “I don’t really need to be out today,” and then the day passes and I haven’t gone. It’s not that anybody there has done anything wrong. It’s more the thought of going there and being out somewhere… I start getting uneasy before I even leave.

And the garage, that one is more direct, I suppose. I don’t like being around the tools much anymore, and especially not over by the place where I used to keep the ladder. Even if I’m only going in there for something small, I notice myself staying away from that side. I’ll tell myself the work can wait, or I don’t have the right energy for it, but really I just don’t want to be near it. It sets me off inside some, so I shut the door and leave it alone.
Do you find yourself having thoughts that repeat over and over in your mind, even when you try to stop thinking about them?

Yes… yes, that happens. Not all day every day, maybe, but when something sets it off, it’s hard to get it out of my head.

Like if I hear metal scrape against something — even something simple, like somebody dragging a tool or a chair leg catching wrong — it can just… it jumps me right back. Or if I’m going past a house and there’s a ladder leaning up in the yard, not even my ladder, just any ladder sitting there at the wrong angle, I’ll see it and then my mind goes right back to it.

It’s like for a second I’m under there again, waiting for help. I know I’m not, I know I’m standing right where I am, but my head doesn’t seem to care right away. The picture comes back, and then I keep thinking about it even after I try to push it aside. I’ll tell myself, “Quit it, that’s over, you’re fine,” but it keeps circling around for a while. Sometimes I have to really work to get my mind onto something else.
Do you ever have thoughts that feel like they're forcing their way into your mind, even when you don't want to think about them?

Yes… that’s a good way to put it, I think. It’s not like I sit down and decide to think about it. I’ll be doing something ordinary, or just going along, and then if I hear metal scrape — like a tool dragging or something catching that sharp way — it just pushes right in.

Or if I see a ladder leaning in somebody’s yard, even if it’s not mine and I don’t know the person, my mind doesn’t just notice it and move on. The whole thing comes back in my head. For a moment it’s like I’m under there again, waiting for help, and I don’t want to be thinking about that at all.

I try to tell myself, “You’re not there now,” but the thought kind of forces its way in before I can stop it. It’s not constant, but when it happens, it really does feel like it gets into my head without permission.
Do you feel like these thoughts that come into your mind are a part of you or do they feel like they are coming from outside of yourself?

No… I wouldn’t say it feels like it’s coming from outside me, like somebody else is putting it there. It’s in my own head, I know that.

But it doesn’t feel like I’m choosing it, either. That’s the part that bothers me. I’ll hear that metal scraping sound, or I’ll see a ladder leaning up in somebody’s yard, and before I even have time to think, the whole thing jumps back in my mind. It’s like I’m right back under there again, waiting for help.

So… it’s mine, I guess, but it doesn’t feel under my control. It just comes rushing in.
Have you noticed that your unease or these repeating thoughts are affecting your ability to work or interact with family and friends?

Yes… some. I mean, I’m not falling apart completely or anything. I still get up, wash up, eat, do the basic things I need to do. I can get through the day, mostly. But my day is a lot smaller than it used to be, if that makes sense.

I don’t go to the senior center anymore like I used to. I used to go just to be around people, maybe play cards, talk a little, have coffee. Now I find reasons not to go. And around the house, there are things I just avoid, more than I like to admit. My wife ends up doing chores I used to handle, and I feel bad about that. I’ll tell myself I’m going to do it, then I see something or I start thinking too much, and I just leave it.

And my bridge friends… I don’t visit with them much anymore either. I used to enjoy that. Now it feels easier to stay home, but then staying home makes everything feel even narrower. So yes, it has affected things. Not in a way where I can’t function at all, but enough that my wife notices, and I notice too.
Have you felt like your unease or these thoughts have been affecting your relationships with your family or friends?

Yes… yes, I’d say it has, though maybe not in some big dramatic way. I still do my basic things, you know — I get up, I wash, I eat, I can manage the ordinary routine. But with people… I’ve pulled back more than I meant to.

I don’t go to the senior center anymore, and I used to go there pretty regularly. It was a place to see folks, have coffee, sit and talk. Now I just don’t go. I tell myself I’m not in the mood, or I’ll go next week, but then next week comes and I still stay home.

And with my wife, it affects things around the house. I avoid certain things, or I put them off so long that she ends up doing chores I used to take care of. I don’t like that. It makes me feel like I’m leaving things on her, and that’s not how I want to be.

My bridge friends too… I don’t visit with them much anymore. I used to enjoy that, just sitting with them and playing and talking. Now my days have gotten smaller, I guess. More of my time is just at home, not seeing people the way I used to. So yes, it has affected my relationships some.
Do you feel like these thoughts are intrusive, meaning they come into your mind even when you're trying to think about something else?

Yes… that’s exactly how it feels. I can be thinking about something plain, like what I’m going to eat or whether I need to take the trash out, and then if I hear metal scrape somewhere, it just cuts right through whatever I was thinking.

Or if I’m riding by and see a ladder leaning up in somebody’s yard, even if it has nothing to do with me, the whole thing jumps back in my head before I can stop it. It’s not like I sit there and decide to remember it. It just comes in, and for a moment it feels like I’m under there again, waiting for help.

So yes, I’d call it intrusive. It comes whether I want it to or not.
Have you felt like your unease or these thoughts have been affecting your ability to enjoy activities or hobbies that you used to find pleasurable?

Yes… I think so. I still do a couple of the things I used to like, so it’s not like I’ve stopped everything altogether. I still go out and water the garden, and I’ll fuss with my old radios sometimes, take the back off one and look at the wires, clean a knob, that sort of thing.

But the feeling I used to get from it… that’s what’s changed. Before, watering the garden felt peaceful to me. I’d stand there and look at the plants, notice what was coming up, feel good that I was taking care of something. Now I do it more because it needs doing. Same with the radios. I can still sit there and tinker, but that little enjoyment, that satisfaction when something works again, it doesn’t come like it used to.

It’s hard to explain. I’m doing the motions, but the pleasure part is kind of dulled down. I keep hoping if I keep at it, maybe it’ll feel the way it used to, but most days it just doesn’t.
Do you feel like you have to do certain things in a specific way to feel safe or to prevent something bad from happening?

Yes… I suppose I do, though I don’t know if I’d call it a ritual exactly. It’s more that when I go somewhere now, I can’t just walk in and sit down like I used to.

I find myself looking around first — up above me, at shelves or fixtures or anything that looks like it could come loose or fall. Then I notice where the exits are, even if it’s just a little room or somebody’s house. I look at the floor too, or the steps, to see if they seem steady, if there’s anything uneven or shaky. I’ll stand there a moment longer than I need to, just checking it all with my eyes.

It’s not that I think doing that will magically stop something bad, but I don’t feel settled until I’ve looked. Once I know where things are and that nothing looks ready to give way, then I can sit a little easier. If I don’t do it, I stay tense, like I missed something important.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts are a part of who you are, or do they feel alien to you?

No… I wouldn’t say they feel like they’re part of who I am. They feel more like something that barges in on me.

I mean, I know it’s my mind having the thought, but it doesn’t feel like me choosing it, if that makes sense. I’ll be going along, just minding my business, and then I hear metal scrape somewhere, or I see a ladder leaning in somebody’s yard, and all at once the whole thing jumps back into my head. It’s not like an ordinary memory where you sit and think, “Oh, I remember that.” It comes in hard and sudden, and for a bit it’s like I’m under there again, waiting for help.

That doesn’t feel like me. It feels alien, I guess is the word you used. It feels like something that got stuck in me and keeps coming back up when I don’t want it to.
Have you felt like your symptoms have been impacting your overall quality of life?

Yes… it has. I can still get through my day, mostly. I mean, I get up, wash, eat, do the regular things a man has to do. So it’s not like I’m helpless or anything like that. But my life has gotten… smaller, I guess that’s the best way to say it.

I used to go down to the senior center, not every day, but often enough. I’d sit, talk with people, maybe play a game, have coffee. I don’t do that much anymore. I keep telling myself I’ll go next week, or when I’m feeling more settled, but then I just don’t. Same with my bridge friends. I used to visit with them, and that gave some shape to the week. Now I hardly see them. I miss it, but at the same time I don’t push myself to go.

And around the house, I still do what I can, but there are things I avoid now. Little chores I used to handle without thinking, my wife ends up doing them or reminding me about them. I don’t like that. I’ve always tried to be useful around the house, and it bothers me seeing her take on things that used to be mine.

So yes, overall, I’d say it’s affected the quality of my life. I’m still managing, but I’m not living the same way I was. My days feel more closed in.
Do you feel like your repetitive thoughts or urges to check things are focused on preventing a specific bad thing from happening, like an accident or harm to yourself or others?

Yes, I think it is aimed at that, in a way. Not like I believe I can control everything, but it’s mostly about making sure something isn’t going to fall, or that I’m not going to get caught somewhere if something gives way.

When I go places now, I don’t just sit down. I look around first. I look up at anything overhead, shelves, lights, whatever might come loose. I check where the exits are, even if it’s just a small room. And I look at the floor or the steps, whether they seem steady or uneven. I need to see those things before I can feel at ease.

So yes, it’s specific in that sense. I’m checking for danger, I suppose — things falling, a way out, whether where I’m standing is safe. If I don’t look, I feel like I’ve left myself open to something happening.
Do you often feel extremely tired or lacking in energy, even after getting enough rest?

I’m not sure I’d say “extremely” tired, no. I mean, I’m 74, so I don’t expect to feel like I did when I was a young man, and some days I move slower than others. That feels pretty ordinary to me.

If I’ve had a busy day, or I’ve been out running errands, then sure, I’ll sit down and feel worn out. But I haven’t really noticed that I’m exhausted even after resting, not in a way that stands out to me. Most mornings, if I’ve slept enough, I can get up and do the usual things. Maybe not with a spring in my step, but I can manage.

So… no, I don’t think that’s been one of the main problems for me.
Do you feel like your symptoms are significantly interfering with your daily life or causing you a lot of distress?

Yes, it does interfere, though I wouldn’t say I’m falling apart or anything like that. I still manage my basic routine. I get up, get washed, eat, take care of the ordinary things a person has to do in a day. So from the outside maybe it doesn’t look so serious.

But it has changed my life. I don’t go to the senior center much anymore, and that used to be part of my week. I’d see people, talk a little, have coffee, just be around others. Now I keep putting it off. And I don’t visit with my bridge friends the way I used to either, so there are fewer things to look forward to.

Around the house, too, I avoid certain things now, enough that my wife ends up doing chores I used to handle myself. That bothers me. I don’t like feeling like I’ve handed things over to her when I should still be able to do them.

So yes… it’s not that I can’t function at all, but my days have gotten smaller. And that is distressing, because I notice it. I know I’m not living the way I used to.
Do you feel compelled to perform any specific rituals or behaviors in order to reduce your anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Yes… I suppose I do, though I don’t think of it like a ritual exactly. It’s more like something I have to do before I can settle myself.

When I go somewhere now, I can’t just walk in and sit down like I used to. I’ll look around first — not in a dramatic way, but I’m checking. I look up to see if there’s anything overhead that looks like it could fall, like shelves or lights or whatever’s hanging there. Then I look for where the exits are, even if it’s a place I’ve been before. And I pay attention to the floor or the steps, whether they look steady, whether there’s anything uneven.

If I don’t do that, I feel on edge, like I’m sitting there without knowing whether I’m safe. Once I’ve looked, I can breathe a little easier and sit down, but it’s not really a choice anymore. It’s become part of how I enter a place.

doctor.question: Do you ever have thoughts that feel like they're forcing their way into your mind, even when you don't want to think about them?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when I hear metal scrape or see a ladder leaning in somebody's yard, the whole thing jumps back in my head like I'm under there again waiting for help.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about unwanted thoughts that force their way into the mind, which directly matches intrusive, involuntary distressing memories of the traumatic event.

patient.answer:
Yes… that’s a good way to put it, I think. It’s not like I sit down and decide to think about it. I’ll be doing something ordinary, or just going along, and then if I hear metal scrape — like a tool dragging or something catching that sharp way — it just pushes right in.

Or if I see a ladder leaning in somebody’s yard, even if it’s not mine and I don’t know the person, my mind doesn’t just notice it and move on. The whole thing comes back in my head. For a moment it’s like I’m under there again, waiting for help, and I don’t want to be thinking about that at all.

I try to tell myself, “You’re not there now,” but the thought kind of forces its way in before I can stop it. It’s not constant, but when it happens, it really does feel like it gets into my head without permission.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's thoughts are intrusive and ego-dystonic
doctor.question: Do you feel like these thoughts that come into your mind are a part of you or do they feel like they are coming from outside of yourself?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when I hear metal scrape or see a ladder leaning in somebody's yard, the whole thing jumps back in my head like I'm under there again waiting for help.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the intrusive thoughts already described and whether they feel internally generated or external; this most directly relates to recurrent involuntary trauma memories.

patient.answer:
No… I wouldn’t say it feels like it’s coming from outside me, like somebody else is putting it there. It’s in my own head, I know that.

But it doesn’t feel like I’m choosing it, either. That’s the part that bothers me. I’ll hear that metal scraping sound, or I’ll see a ladder leaning up in somebody’s yard, and before I even have time to think, the whole thing jumps back in my mind. It’s like I’m right back under there again, waiting for help.

So… it’s mine, I guess, but it doesn’t feel under my control. It just comes rushing in.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Have you noticed that your unease or these repeating thoughts are affecting your ability to work or interact with family and friends?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still manage my basic routines, but I’ve stopped going to the senior center and I avoid enough things around the house that my wife has to handle chores I used to do. I also don’t visit with my bridge friends much anymore, so my days have gotten smaller.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms are affecting daily functioning and relationships with family and friends, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… some. I mean, I’m not falling apart completely or anything. I still get up, wash up, eat, do the basic things I need to do. I can get through the day, mostly. But my day is a lot smaller than it used to be, if that makes sense.

I don’t go to the senior center anymore like I used to. I used to go just to be around people, maybe play cards, talk a little, have coffee. Now I find reasons not to go. And around the house, there are things I just avoid, more than I like to admit. My wife ends up doing chores I used to handle, and I feel bad about that. I’ll tell myself I’m going to do it, then I see something or I start thinking too much, and I just leave it.

And my bridge friends… I don’t visit with them much anymore either. I used to enjoy that. Now it feels easier to stay home, but then staying home makes everything feel even narrower. So yes, it has affected things. Not in a way where I can’t function at all, but enough that my wife notices, and I notice too.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning

target_item.name: Functional Impairment

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms are affecting relationships and social functioning with family or friends, which is directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I’d say it has, though maybe not in some big dramatic way. I still do my basic things, you know — I get up, I wash, I eat, I can manage the ordinary routine. But with people… I’ve pulled back more than I meant to.

I don’t go to the senior center anymore, and I used to go there pretty regularly. It was a place to see folks, have coffee, sit and talk. Now I just don’t go. I tell myself I’m not in the mood, or I’ll go next week, but then next week comes and I still stay home.

And with my wife, it affects things around the house. I avoid certain things, or I put them off so long that she ends up doing chores I used to take care of. I don’t like that. It makes me feel like I’m leaving things on her, and that’s not how I want to be.

My bridge friends too… I don’t visit with them much anymore. I used to enjoy that, just sitting with them and playing and talking. Now my days have gotten smaller, I guess. More of my time is just at home, not seeing people the way I used to. So yes, it has affected my relationships some.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of obsessive thoughts
doctor.question: Do you feel like these thoughts are intrusive, meaning they come into your mind even when you're trying to think about something else?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when I hear metal scrape or see a ladder leaning in somebody's yard, the whole thing jumps back in my head like I'm under there again waiting for help.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the thoughts come into the mind involuntarily and intrusively, even when trying to think about something else.

patient.answer:
Yes… that’s exactly how it feels. I can be thinking about something plain, like what I’m going to eat or whether I need to take the trash out, and then if I hear metal scrape somewhere, it just cuts right through whatever I was thinking.

Or if I’m riding by and see a ladder leaning up in somebody’s yard, even if it has nothing to do with me, the whole thing jumps back in my head before I can stop it. It’s not like I sit there and decide to remember it. It just comes in, and for a moment it feels like I’m under there again, waiting for help.

So yes, I’d call it intrusive. It comes whether I want it to or not.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Have you felt like your unease or these thoughts have been affecting your ability to enjoy activities or hobbies that you used to find pleasurable?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: I still water the garden and tinker with old radios some, but the good feeling I used to get from it just doesn't come like it did.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms affect enjoyment of previously pleasurable activities or hobbies, which most directly matches reduced ability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I still do a couple of the things I used to like, so it’s not like I’ve stopped everything altogether. I still go out and water the garden, and I’ll fuss with my old radios sometimes, take the back off one and look at the wires, clean a knob, that sort of thing.

But the feeling I used to get from it… that’s what’s changed. Before, watering the garden felt peaceful to me. I’d stand there and look at the plants, notice what was coming up, feel good that I was taking care of something. Now I do it more because it needs doing. Same with the radios. I can still sit there and tinker, but that little enjoyment, that satisfaction when something works again, it doesn’t come like it used to.

It’s hard to explain. I’m doing the motions, but the pleasure part is kind of dulled down. I keep hoping if I keep at it, maybe it’ll feel the way it used to, but most days it just doesn’t.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of compulsions to perform specific rituals or behaviors
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have to do certain things in a specific way to feel safe or to prevent something bad from happening?

target_item.name: Hypervigilance
target_item.manifestation: When I go places now I look around for what might fall, where the exits are, and whether the floor or steps look steady before I can sit easy.
target_item.reason: The question asks about safety-related behaviors done to feel safe or prevent harm, which best matches being persistently alert and checking the environment for danger.

patient.answer:
Yes… I suppose I do, though I don’t know if I’d call it a ritual exactly. It’s more that when I go somewhere now, I can’t just walk in and sit down like I used to.

I find myself looking around first — up above me, at shelves or fixtures or anything that looks like it could come loose or fall. Then I notice where the exits are, even if it’s just a little room or somebody’s house. I look at the floor too, or the steps, to see if they seem steady, if there’s anything uneven or shaky. I’ll stand there a moment longer than I need to, just checking it all with my eyes.

It’s not that I think doing that will magically stop something bad, but I don’t feel settled until I’ve looked. Once I know where things are and that nothing looks ready to give way, then I can sit a little easier. If I don’t do it, I stay tense, like I missed something important.

patient.answer:
No… I wouldn’t say they feel like they’re part of who I am. They feel more like something that barges in on me.

I mean, I know it’s my mind having the thought, but it doesn’t feel like me choosing it, if that makes sense. I’ll be going along, just minding my business, and then I hear metal scrape somewhere, or I see a ladder leaning in somebody’s yard, and all at once the whole thing jumps back into my head. It’s not like an ordinary memory where you sit and think, “Oh, I remember that.” It comes in hard and sudden, and for a bit it’s like I’m under there again, waiting for help.

That doesn’t feel like me. It feels alien, I guess is the word you used. It feels like something that got stuck in me and keeps coming back up when I don’t want it to.

doctor.question: Do you feel like your repetitive thoughts or urges to check things are focused on preventing a specific bad thing from happening, like an accident or harm to yourself or others?

target_item.name: Hypervigilance
target_item.manifestation: When I go places now I look around for what might fall, where the exits are, and whether the floor or steps look steady before I can sit easy.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about checking the environment to prevent accidents or harm, which most directly matches being persistently alert and tense about surroundings.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think it is aimed at that, in a way. Not like I believe I can control everything, but it’s mostly about making sure something isn’t going to fall, or that I’m not going to get caught somewhere if something gives way.

When I go places now, I don’t just sit down. I look around first. I look up at anything overhead, shelves, lights, whatever might come loose. I check where the exits are, even if it’s just a small room. And I look at the floor or the steps, whether they seem steady or uneven. I need to see those things before I can feel at ease.

So yes, it’s specific in that sense. I’m checking for danger, I suppose — things falling, a way out, whether where I’m standing is safe. If I don’t look, I feel like I’ve left myself open to something happening.

I’m not sure I’d say “extremely” tired, no. I mean, I’m 74, so I don’t expect to feel like I did when I was a young man, and some days I move slower than others. That feels pretty ordinary to me.

Maybe not with a spring in my step, but I can manage.

So… no, I don’t think that’s been one of the main problems for me.
